title: Structure-Tunable Copper-Indium Catalysts for Highly Selective CO2 Electroreduction to CO or HCOOH
abstract: Selectively approaching chemicals with one compositiontunable catalyst is attractive for the practical manufacturing. In this work, bimetallic copper-indium (Cu-In) catalysts were synthesized for the electrochemical CO2 reduction to CO or HCOOH, both are among the best In-based catalysts reported in the literature. For the first time, we report that by varying the metal ratio, the catalyst can be tuned from a core-shell structure that selectively produces CO to a well-mixed structure that prefers HCOOH production. The distinct selectivities were found to depend on the structure-sensitive binding strength of key reactive intermediates. Our findings can benefit the development of a broader range of selectivity-tunable catalysts. The increasing environmental concerns have triggered tremendous efforts to transform CO2 greenhouse gas into fuels and value-added commodity chemicals in order to achieve carbon neutrality and a sustainable society. Thermalcatalytically, CO2 can be hydrogenated with molecular hydrogen to a variety of products such as alcohols, alkanes, alkenes, esters, aromatics, etc. However, these reactions typically proceed under harsh conditions . Alternatively, CO2 can be electrocatalytically reduced with water as the hydrogen atom source and renewable electricity as the energy input. Attributed to the mild operating conditions, such processes also favor small-scale modular manufacturing locally and on-demand to match the distributed carbon feedstocks. However, lack of inexpensive electrocatalysts that can afford high activity, selectivity and durability have greatly hampered the technological advances. Numerous types of catalysts were reported to direct CO2 electroreduction towards different target molecules. Pure metal catalysts, such as Au, Ag and Pd , were found to be active for CO2 reduction to CO; [13] while Sn, In and Pb are able to convert CO2 to HCOOH at high Faradaic efficiencies. Other types of catalysts include molecular complexes (phthalocyanine, porphyrin, etc.), single atom catalysts and metal-free catalysts. For instances, supported cobalt phthalocyanines on carbon nanotubes were demonstrated to be active for CO production at a high Faradaic efficiency of > 95%. And copper phthalocyanines are selective for CH4 with a Faradaic efficiency of 66%. While carbon-based metal-free materials, such as nitrogen-doped graphene quantum dots (NGQDs), were reported to yield C2 products such as ethylene and ethanol. Cu, on the other hand, is the only known metal that is capable to reduce CO2 into hydrocarbons. Depending on the surface morphology, structure, oxidation status or even operating conditions, the main products can range from C1 products such as CO, CH4, CH3OH and HCOOH to C3 products such as npropanol. The selectivity of Cu catalysts can also be effectively tuned by alloying with other metals, which is thought to alter the binding energies of the key intermediates towards CO2 reduction. For example, a Cu-Pd bimetallic catalyst was shown to produce CO with a Faradaic efficiency of 86% at -0.89 V vs. RHE. By alloying with Sn, the catalyst can selectively produce HCOOH with high Faradaic efficiencies. A nanoporous Cu-Ag alloy catalyst was synthesized using an electrodeposition method, showing high Faradaic efficiencies for the production of C2H4 (60%) and C2H5OH (25%) at -0.7 V vs. RHE. Bimetallic catalysts comprising Cu and In have recently received much attention, attributed to their outstanding selectivities towards CO. However, CO is the only target molecule that can be selectively produced. In this work, we synthesized bimetallic Cu-In catalysts using a co-precipitation method. Our catalysts can not only selectively produce CO, by altering the Cu/In molar ratio, the product can be altered to HCOOH at a high Faradaic efficiency. The structural evolutions of the catalysts during the reaction and their intrinsic correlation to the selectivity divergence were elucidated with a series of material characterizations and density function theory (DFT) calculations. To prepare the supported Cu-In catalyst, calculated amounts of metal precursors and carbon nanotubes (CNTs) were dissolved/dispersed in H2O. Under vigorous stirring, 50 mM of the NaOH solution was drop-wisely added until a complete precipitation was achieved. The precipitate was then washed with H2O and vacuum-dried overnight at 60°C. We optimized the molecular ratio of Cu/In and screened two catalysts for further discussions: Cu94In6 with a Cu/In ratio of 15:1 and Cu25In75 with a Cu/In ratio of 1:3. Pure Cu and In catalysts supported on the CNTs were also synthesized for a parallel comparison. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images show welldispersed nanoparticles attached to the sidewall of CNTs (Figure 1a-b). A detailed HR-TEM analysis on Cu25In75 reveals dominating disordered species with only small regions of orientated patterns originating from CuO (Figure 1c). The bulk structure and crystallinity were further investigated with X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis, which clearly show the CuO phase in Cu/CNT and the In(OH)3 phase in In/CNT (Figure 1d). The Cu(OH)2 initially formed during the precipitation is unstable and tend to decompose into CuO at elevated temperatures. When both Cu and In are present, the intensities of CuO and In(OH)3 signals decrease dramatically. This is consistent with the HRTEM results that a majority part of the bimetallic particles is amorphous.
